amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁעַ` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once at the head of the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָּזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְּרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone.
amendments.why: EZK.13.7 is the case rule 25 had not considered: `הֲלוֹא` is written once and the ASV rewrites both the fronted auxiliary and the negation for the second of two coordinated questions. Rule 25's existing text said `phrases`, which leaves a verse pass to choose between two `added` units and folding the repeats into the second verb, both of which lose a written morpheme's own realization. Rule 55 already reads a rewritten אֲשֶׁר or כִּי exactly this way and points at rule 25 for the mechanism, so the widening is the generalisation that rule already assumes rather than a new principle. The closing limit keeps it clear of rule 35's gapping, which the same chapter exercises at 13.5, where no negative morpheme stands in the second clause and the waw alone carries neither.

conventions: אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (8 occurrences: 13.3, 13.8 twice, 13.9, 13.13, 13.16, 13.18, 13.20) is aligned as three units and always the same way: the supplied the joins אֲדֹנָי as the nominal it determines (rules 15, 29), the 1cs suffix on אֲדֹנָי is unrepresented because the ASV writes no my, and יְהֹוִה takes Jehovah. Where the formula is the predicate of a verbless clause the copula joins אֲדֹנָי with the the (13.9, am the Lord). This is the chapter's largest BSB divergence and is convention, not error: BSB renders that suffix.

The daub idiom (13.10, 13.11, 13.12, 13.14, 13.15) is read one way throughout. תָּפֵל is one substantive rendered untempered mortar, headed on untempered (rule 31). The with by which the English verb reaches that bare accusative joins the verb's or participle's unit, discontinuous around whatever stands between (rule 44). An English it after the verb goes to a present אֵת+suffix (13.10 s024, 13.15 s014) and is its own added unit where no suffix stands (13.11 t006, 13.12 t022); it is never folded into the verb's rendering.

A supplied with before a bare accusative divides by what the Hebrew noun is, not by the English word. The second accusative of the double-accusative טוּחַ (13.10, 13.11, 13.14, 13.15) and the object of בָּקַע (13.13) take it into the verb's unit under rule 44; the adverbial accusative שֶׁקֶר of 13.22, whose verb already has its own rendered object, keeps it under rule 33. Read which the noun is before placing the word.

Follow MACULA's article tokens rather than the pointing when placing the ASV's the after a pointed preposition. 13.5 (s004, s015) and 13.15 (s007, s011) carry a bracketed [הַ] that takes the written the (rule 12), while 13.4's בָּ is tagged R with no article token of any kind, so its supplied the belongs to the nominal expression it determines (rule 15) and rule 30 has nothing to fuse. This is a correction already applied to 13.4 and is the reading for the whole chapter.

no more is split where both morphemes are written and whole where only one is. In 13.21 and 13.23 לֹא takes no and עוֹד takes more, including 13.23 where the ASV moves more forward into the earlier clause (rule 25). In 13.15, where no עוֹד stands, the existential אַיִן takes is no more entire and heads on the negation (rule 50).

report: Checked all 48 candidate lemma groups, then read the dump end to end for the splits the table is blind to (added units, folded supplies). No construction in this chapter is analysed two ways without something in the source or in the ASV's own wording licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

The multi-treatment buckets are ASV-driven rather than splits. A waw before a 1cs qatal is even/Thus/So/and/also because those are the words the ASV wrote (rule 14's open list; 13.21's postpositive also is rule 51). אֶל, עַל and מִן follow the written word the same way. הַ on a participle is a bare relative where an explicit noun is modified (13.6, 13.9, 13.16, 13.17) and a supplied pronoun with a relative where the participle is substantival (13.15) — rule 41 against rule 46, and the morphology decides which.

The chapter's one recurring idiom is uniform in all five verses that carry it: טוּחַ + תָּפֵל gives the supplied with to the verb (rule 44 names this very idiom), reads תָּפֵל as one substantive headed on untempered (rule 31), aligns the English it to a present אֵת+suffix (13.10, 13.15), and marks it added where no suffix stands (13.11, 13.12). The four added it and two added them across 13.11–13.13 and 13.20 are that same reading applied consistently; none is folded into a neighbouring verb.

The one boundary a later reader could mistake for a split is the supplied with: it joins the verb's unit for the double-accusative טוּחַ (13.10, 13.11, 13.14, 13.15) and בָּקַע (13.13), and joins the noun for 13.22's adverbial accusative שֶׁקֶר. That is the line rule 44's last limit draws against rule 33; both verse notes cite the rule they used, so I left both accepted and recorded the boundary as a convention.

13.16's added to wit and 13.20's אֵת → even are the two halves of rule 16's limit correctly applied: 13.20's marker stands on the appositive itself, and 13.16 writes no marker on the fronted phrase at all. 13.22's closing and is added on the same principle under rule 14, since that clause has no conjunction morpheme in it.

13.4's bare בָּ against the bracketed [הַ] of 13.5 and 13.15 is a morphology difference, not a split: MACULA supplies an article token in the latter two and none in the former, so 13.4's supplied the belongs to the noun (rule 15) and the other four the's belong to their article tokens (rule 12). Recorded as a convention, since the pointing alone would suggest the opposite.

BSB: all 22 disagreements are documented convention differences and none is an error. Nine Sp1cs are the אֲדֹנָי suffix (eight) plus 13.18's elbows, which the ASV does not render; five R are לֵאמֹר (rule 27) and the recast לְ of 13.3, 13.22 (rule 40); three To are ordinary object markers (rule 16); three הַ are the agreement article of 13.3 (rule 47), the unrendered article of 13.18 (rule 29), and 13.22's article outranked by the suffix's determiner (rule 41); the remaining two are 13.22's relative-recast waw and its dropped object suffix.

Validation flagged 76 notes repeating across verses with 0 conventions recorded. Five conventions returned here cover the ones a verse aligned from the log alone would otherwise have to rediscover; the rest are per-verse restatements of contract rules and need no entry.
One amendment: rule 25, widened to cover a particle whose scope spans coordinated clauses, on 13.7's הֲלוֹא written once and rewritten by the ASV as Have ... not twice.
